title: Esther
versionTitle: Esther; Based on Malbim. Trans. Moshe Atlas, 2026
text:
Once upon a time, in the days of a commoner called Ahasuerus.
He married Vashti, a scion of the powerful Babylonian conqueror Nebuchadnezzar, and thereby suddenly became King Ahasuerus, the ruler of a vast empire – of one hundred and twenty-seven provinces – from India in the East to North-West Africa in the West.

It happened in those early days, when King Ahasuerus ascended his very own royal throne which he had audaciously relocated in his new capital city, the Shushan fortress, to display his individual might and disdain for the royal tradition.

In the third year of his attempt to remodel the monarchy and transition from law-abiding king to above-the-law dictator, he made a banquet to further this cause.
First and foremost, his banquet was for all his officials and courtiers, and members of the Persian and Median military. Then, he also invited the nobles and provincial officials that had previously held office.
The hierarchical manner of these invitations was intended to make a powerful political statement: the lawmakers of the past were now the subdued and obedient subjects of Ahasuerus’ military rule.

Moreover, at this banquet, he flaunted the national treasures as though they were his own. He presented them as personal wealth befitting his honourable kingship, and lavishness befitting his magnificent greatness. He brazenly did this for many days – one hundred and eighty in total.

After successfully completing these one hundred and eighty days of festivities, the king made a further seven-day banquet for all the common folk that lived in the environs of the Shushan fortress, from the highest-ranking to lowest-ranking. He held it in the courtyard of the king’s palatial gardens, where no commoner had previously been permitted to set foot. He did this to further demonstrate his disdain for tradition and convention, along with his disregard for the privileges the nobility had hitherto enjoyed.

For this banquet, he constructed a most extravagant marquee: It had tenting of white and indigo-blue cotton that was held in place by ropes of fine linen and purple and supported by silver cylinders and alabaster columns. It was furnished with couches of silver and gold, laid out on flooring of marble, alabaster, mother-of-pearl, and mosaic.

And the drinks were served in sets of golden vessels, of which there were so many that each guest received his own set. And there was a vast supply of delicious wine that was fit for a king, as befits a king’s financial ability.

To further upend the stature of the nobility, he dispensed with the customary toasts: The drinking policy was that nobody should be forced to toast to his superiors, for this was the king’s instruction to all the important members of his court: “Let each man behave as he pleases”.

To demonstrate that Queen Vashti was queen by virtue of being his wife, rather than him being king by virtue of being her husband, she also made a banquet, but only for the women, and she was made to hold it in the royal quarters that belonged to King Ahasuerus, rather than in her own quarters.

Moreover, on the seventh and final day of the banquet, when the king was merry with wine, he decided to publicly exhibit that he had only married Vashti for her good looks and had no regard for her royal lineage. And so, he instructed Mehuman, Bizzeta, Charvona, Bigta, Avagta, Zetar, and Charcas, the seven valets who were the personal attendants of King Ahasuerus –

To bring Vashti the Queen to stand before the king, and then place the crown on her head in his presence. This was intended to show the nations and the officials that she was only queen by virtue of being his wife, and that he had chosen her as his wife solely because she was beautiful, for indeed she was very good looking.
Through this blatant act of disparaging the royal family into which he had married, Ahasuerus hoped to unequivocally demonstrate to his subjects that he had broken with past conventions. From now on, he would autonomously determine policy without restraint.
But Vashti felt entitled to be the queen by virtue of her royal lineage, and so she refused to come. She refused to belittle herself by obeying the king’s disrespectful command, and to submit herself to being handled by his lowly valets rather than her personal chambermaids.
The king was outwardly furious that she had publicly humiliated him, and inwardly aggrieved that she had ruined his politically-motivated exhibition.

However, the king loved her dearly and wished to spare her from punishment. And so the king informed the wise fellows of the royal court assigned to her trial, who combined legal expertise with an appreciation of contextual factors, that although this case involves slighting the king, it was a marital feud that could just as well be heard by any commoners’ court that appreciates morality as well as law.

Matters were eased by the fact that he was well acquainted with the judges assigned to the case. Their names were Carshena, Shetar, Admata, Tarshish, Meres, Marsena, and Memuchan. They were the seven officials of Persia and Media who frequently saw the king, with the foremost experience in the royal court.
He therefore hoped that they would cooperate with his attempts to secure Vashti’s acquittal and hush up the case.

He emphasized that he sought a morally sensitive ruling on how to respond to Queen Vashti who was herself a royal, and had perhaps only disobeyed King Ahasuerus’ order because it had been disrespectfully sent in the hands of his valets.

However, much to the king’s dismay, Memuchan loudly proclaimed in the presence of the king and the officials that Vashti’s crime could not be hushed up, because her disobedience was far more serious than a commoner’s marital feud. Firstly, he argued that Vashti was only the queen by virtue of being Ahasuerus’ wife – her noncompliance risked derailing the king’s ambitions to cement his dictatorship. Secondly, he argued that she did not only commit an offense against the king, but also against all the officials and all the peoples in all the provinces of King Ahasuerus – she set a terrible precedent for all women throughout the empire.

How so? Because word of the queen’s behavior will spread amongst all the women throughout the empire, and will cause them to view their husbands with condescension. Because they will reason: If King Ahasuerus commanded that Queen Vashti merely be brought before him, and yet she was defiant and would not come, all the more so ought we to defy our commoner husbands’ tough and unreasonable demands!
The masses will interpret Vashti’s behaviour as a simple act of feminine defiance, since they will fail to realize the political significance of Vashti’s refusal.

And because already today the court ladies of Persia and Media who heard the queen’s outburst will relay news of her political defiance to all the king’s officials, and there will be enormous disgrace and outcry! The nobility will realize that Ahasuerus’ dictatorial ambitions are contested even within his own palace.

But do not worry! I have a plan to right these two wrongs; to salvage the king’s dictatorial ambitions and to reassert male authority among the commoner masses.
If it seems good to the king, from now on all governmental directives should be personally issued by him, and codified, for eternity, in the legal traditions of Persia and Media. From now on, the king shall formally reside above the law; he shall become the empire’s supreme lawmaker.
Then, the king should utilize his new powers and decree that Vashti shall never again appear before King Ahasuerus.
Finally, the king should hand over her royal title to a commoner who is more desirable as a woman than her. Find a new wife, and emphasize character and beauty over lineage and bloodline. She will certainly be mindful of Vashti’s fate and treat you with the utmost respect, just as a good wife should.

If only the king will follow my counsel, from now on all legal directives advanced by the king will resound throughout the empire, because his monarchy shall stand supreme above the law. And all the women will treat their husbands with respect, be they high-ranking or low-ranking. Even women who married lower-ranking men than themselves will think twice after learning of the venerable Vashti’s fate.

And this seemed like a good plan in the eyes of the king and his inner circle of officials. The king then autonomously implemented Memuchan’s plan.
Thus the revolution was formalized; the seven top governmental officials resigned their legislative powers to the king who immediately acted upon them.

He dispatched legal scrolls, and addressed them to all the countries of “the king’s empire”. They were no longer to be known as the “Persian and Median empire”; the king had radically broken with the conventions of the past, and now they were accountable to him alone.
Moreover, he had each country’s scroll written in its own alphabet, and each nation’s scroll in its own language. By not writing in the empire’s formal script and tongue, he further demonstrated his break with the past, and that from now on all his subjects were to be equally subjugated.
The scrolls decreed that each man shall have dictatorial powers over his household whereas each woman shall be deprived of all rights. This edict attempted to counter the negative repercussions of Vashti’s behaviour.
Moreover, they commanded that all formal communications with government shall now be conducted in one’s native language. This edict would be a constant reminder that the status quo of the “Persian and Median empire” had been abolished; from now on each country would be personally accountable to King Ahasuerus alone.

Sometime later, when King Ahasuerus’ anger had been calmed, he remembered with longing his beautiful and influential Vashti, the nature of the offense she had committed, and the harsh consequences that were decreed on her.
Realizing how unfairly and disproportionately she had been treated, he feared that no woman of Vashti’s calibre would dare enter into marriage with him.
When the king’s young menservants learned of his concerns, they said: Let the government issue a public appeal to provide the king with good-looking virgin young women.

And should the young women fail to come forward of their own accord, the king can appoint administrators in each province of his empire, and they can forcibly gather all the good-looking virgin young women and transport them to the harem located in the Shushan fortress.
To train their obedience and ensure that they do not become arrogant, they shall be tended to by a simple male valet, Hegai – caretaker of the women. They shall not be permitted to travel with their own cosmetics. Rather, these shall be handed to them by the palace staff to reward good behaviour.

And the young woman who seems worthy in the eyes of the king shall become queen in Vashti’s stead!
It seemed like a good plan to the king, and so he autonomously enacted the relevant policy using his newfound legislative powers.

Now, there was a brave and righteous Jewish man who had lived for some time in the Shushan fortress. His name was Mordechai and he enjoyed royal ancestry; he was the son of Ya’ir, who was son of Shimi, who was son of Kish – the famed father of King Sha’ul – of the tribe of Binyamin.

He had been deported from Jerusalem, among the upper class, lawmaker and artisan deportees that were deported along with Yechanyah, King of Judea. They were deported by Nebuchadnezzar, King of Babylonia.
As a member of the Jewish upper class, a refugee, and a resident of Shushan who lived right near government headquarters, Mordechai had no excuse – neither unworthiness, privilege, or ignorance – to believe that his family was exempt from the king’s edict.
But, motivated by his religious faith and contempt for the crass royal court, he did his best to conceal Esther –

He was the legal guardian of his cousin, whom he had adopted as a daughter when her mother and father died. She was fondly known to all as Hadassah – a fragrant myrtle by virtue of her good deeds, but her real name was Esther. And the young woman had a beautiful figure and was good looking.

And it came to be, when the king pronounced his alluring words to tempt the young women to come forth willingly and then, due to their ineffectiveness, followed this with his decree insisting that they be sent, that many young women were made to gather in the Shushan fortress subject to the care of Hegai. Then, Esther too was forcibly taken to the king’s palace, subject to the care of Hegai the caretaker of the women.

But although Esther had defied the king’s orders and attempted to escape his clutches, she was not punished by Hegai, because the young woman seemed to be the ideal candidate in his eyes, and so she found favour before him and he forgave her.
He was so confident that she would be the next queen that he hastily ordered her cosmetic treatments and provisions, and even summoned a team of seven chambermaids from the king’s palace to tend to her needs, that would befit her once she became queen. And she and her chambermaids received differential treatment in the finest quarters of the harem.

Despite being singled out in this way, Esther would not share her national and familial identity, because Mordechai had instructed her not to share it. They hoped that Esther’s avoidance of discussing her lineage would lead the officials to presume she was a bastard and expel her from the harem.

But this strategy also risked antagonizing the court, and Mordechai was concerned that Esther’s concerted efforts to avoid the king would be viewed as treasonous and severely punished. And so, every single day Mordechai would walk about in front of the court of the harem, to learn of Esther’s wellbeing and what they intended to do with her. Thankfully, Esther’s charm stood her in good stead, and she survived unscathed.

When each young woman’s turn came to go to King Ahasuerus – this would take place following her successful completion of a twelve month probation period prescribed for the women to ensure that they were healthy and not susceptible to any seasonal sicknesses, neither throughout the six cold months when they would warm themselves with oil of myrrh, nor throughout the six hot months when they would mask unpleasant body odours with perfumes and women’s cosmetics –

With this alone – beauty, trained obedience and a statement of clean health – the young woman would go to the king, because there were no other virtues that he deemed pertinent. Moreover, to encourage consensualness and agreeableness, she would be granted whatever she requested to bring along with her, during her transfer from the harem to the royal palace to commence her life as the king’s mistress.

And thus, the young woman went willingly even though her moment in the spotlight was short-lived. She would arrive in the evening and return in the morning to a second harem under the care of Sha’ashgaz, the king’s valet, caretaker of the concubines. She would not have a further opportunity to go to the king unless he desired her, whereupon she would be summoned by name.

But when the turn of Esther, the daughter of Avichayil, the uncle of Mordechai – who had subsequently adopted her as his daughter – came to go to the king, she did things differently. She requested no gifts to clearly communicate that she did not consent. She only took what Hegai the king’s valet and caretaker of the women personally instructed her to take. But, once again, due to her unique combination of beauty with refinement of character and intellect imbibed from her childhood home, Esther’s defiance went unpunished. On the contrary, she won the admiration of all who saw her.
And Esther had to be taken by force to King Ahasuerus, transported to his quarters within the palace. This took place in the tenth month – the month of Tevet, in the seventh year of his reign.

And the king loved Esther more than all the women he had met, and he admired her and felt more kindly toward her than to all the other virgin candidates. And so, without further ado, he personally placed the royal crown on her head and appointed her queen in Vashti’s stead.

Esther’s secretiveness regarding her identity fascinated the king. He was consumed with curiosity, and attempted to cajole her into revealing it. To this end, the king threw a great banquet for all his officials and courtiers and called it “the banquet of Esther.” He hoped that she would be embarrassed to present herself to the adoring public as an identity-less bastard. He also proclaimed tax remissions for the provinces and distributed gifts as befits a king. He hoped that she would be tempted to reveal at least her national identity in order to take full advantage of the king’s generosity and secure a good package for her people.

Upon seeing that Esther would not yield, he hypothesized that underlying anxiety was at play. Perhaps she feared that disclosing an undesirable identity would lead the king to search for another wife. So, he arranged that the virgin young women were rounded up for a second time – this time from their quarters in the harem – and sent home. Now Esther had nothing to fear.
Moreover, Mordechai – her adoptive parent – was appointed to sit in the king’s court that was located near the royal gates. Hopefully, Esther would reveal her identity to secure even better privileges for Mordechai.

But, all his attempts were in vain. Esther would not reveal her family or national identity, just as Mordechai had instructed her; because Esther followed Mordechai’s opinion as she had done while living with him as an adoptee.
Esther held her sage uncle in such esteem, that she willingly embraced risk to heed his bidding.

How providential that precisely around this time, Mordechai was fulfilling his new role and sitting at the royal gates, when Bigtan and Teresh – two of the king’s valets tasked with guarding the threshold to his quarters – outwardly expressed their fury with the king to one another, and plotted to attack King Ahasuerus.
But, being in the right place at the right time, the plot became known to Mordechai, and he relayed it to Queen Esther. Esther then informed the king in the name of Mordechai.

The poisonous substance was sought and discovered, and they were both indicted of attempt to murder the king and hanged on a stake.
Providentially, this episode was recorded in the king’s private diary rather in the formal royal chronicles, where it would likely have been erased by Haman. Providentially, the king chose to record Mordechai’s favor rather than repay it immediately, which would stand Mordechai and the Jewish people in good stead, as events unfold. And, how providential that only once the infrastructure for the Jew’s ultimate salvation was firmly in place – in the form of Esther and Mordechai’s relationships with the king – did Haman rise to power and endeavour to harm them.

Sometime after the previous events, King Ahasuerus successively promoted Haman son of Hammedata the Agagite. He ultimately offered him the loftiest position in his government and placed his chair higher than those of all his fellow officials.

The grandeur got to Haman’s head and he came to view himself as a demigod. Due to his insistence, all the king’s courtiers, even those working within the palace gates, would kneel and prostrate before Haman, because he had the king order this on his behalf. But Mordechai would not kneel or prostrate. As a Jewish leader, he thought it religiously unacceptable to honour a demigod in this manner.

The courtiers of the king that were situated at the royal gates and tasked with enforcing this new law admonished Mordechai: “Why do you violate the king’s command?” But Mordechai stuck to his principles and disobeyed them.

One day, when their patience wore thin after admonishing him day after day while he continued to disobey them – citing his Jewishness as the reason – they informed Haman, and requested that he overtly visit Mordechai to see whether Mordechai’s excuse was valid.1Here the term לראות is translated forwards and backwards.
They reasoned that Mordechai’s Jewish sensitivities would not forbid bowing to Haman’s face, despite his demigod status, since it is universal etiquette to bow before all officials. If Mordechai would not bow even to Haman’s face, this would confirm that he was in contempt of the law.

And Haman visited Mordechai and saw2Here the term וירא is translated forwards and backwards. that Mordechai still would not kneel or prostrate himself before him. Clearly, invoking Judaism had been a decoy; in fact, Mordechai refused to humble himself before Haman! Haman was too arrogant to show his affront outwardly, but inwardly he was filled with rage, and became bent on avenging his wounded pride.

Although Haman had been personally affronted by Mordechai, the possibility of laying hands on Mordechai alone seemed pathetic in his eyes. It was beneath his dignity to take some Jew’s disrespectful behaviour to heart.
So, given that he had originally been told about, and displeased by, the religious grounds for Mordechai’s refusal to bow before him, and that these were shared by his entire people, Haman plotted to destroy all the Jews throughout the kingdom of Ahasuerus, because they were Mordechai’s nation. They abided, like him, by such distasteful laws, and by ridding the empire of them, he would settle his score with Mordechai.

And so, shortly thereafter, in the first calendar month, that is, the month of Nisan, in the twelfth year of King Ahasuerus’ reign, the lot was cast before Haman who hoped that the very next day (the 14th) would be an auspicious day for executing his plot. But the lots dragged him from the next possible day (the 14th of Nisan) to the last possible day (the 13th of Iyar). Fearing that the entire coming month was not auspicious, Haman then cast lots to find the ideal month, but the lots dragged him from the first possible month (Nisan) to the last possible month, that is, the twelfth month, the month of Adar.

How providential that the lots literally fell on the latest possible date, buying the Jews maximum time.
Unperturbed by this setback, Haman then went and said to King Ahasuerus: “There is ‘this people’, too insignificant to be named, that does not inhabit its own country or even its own cities, but is instead scattered and assimilated within the other nations throughout the provinces of your empire. Their religion has many doctrines that fundamentally differ from those of all other nations, and is thus a cultural anomaly. Moreover, they disobey the king’s laws even when not strictly required to do so on religious grounds. In this way, they corrode society and encourage civil unrest, and it is not worth the king’s while to let them be.

If it seems good in your eyes, I suggest that you have it written to neutralize them. This will be a simple and inexpensive project, and the taskforce will be so willing that I could raise ten thousand kikars of silver from them to invest in the king’s treasuries.”
Haman hoped that his ambiguous terminology, “neutralize”, would be understood by Ahasuerus as cultural reformation and re-education policy. In fact, Haman held a far more sinister interpretation in mind – to neutralize them through genocide. As for the second half of his statement, while it contextually implied to Ahasuerus the willingness of the taskforce, Haman was in fact eyeing the vast loot of the massacred Jews and fantasizing of the plunder tax it would raise.

And indeed, the king fell prey to Haman’s ploy. He had no idea that Haman planned a genocide, and for a people no less significant than the Jews. So, the king removed his signet ring from his hand, and passed it to Haman son of Hammedata the Agagite, the foe of the Jews – scion of a famous Jew-hating family.
Moreover, the king gratefully said to Haman, I will provide you with the necessary silver and you may act against this nation however you see fit.

And lest the king uncover his deception before it was too late, on that very day, on the thirteenth day of the first month - Nisan, the king’s scribes were summoned, and proclamations were written as per Haman’s instructions. They were addressed to the king’s satraps, and to the governors of every province, and to the officials of every nation. They wrote to every province in its own script and to every people in its own language, because typically, many dialects were spoken in each province, but all shared a script. The orders were issued in the name of King Ahasuerus and sealed with the king’s signet.

And, he immediately dispatched them as scrolls with the high-speed couriers to all the king’s provinces.
And this is what they proclaimed: “To destroy, massacre, and neutralize all the Jews, from the young to the old, children and women, on a single day, on the thirteenth day of the twelfth month – that is, the month of Adar – and to plunder their possessions.”
Cunningly, he personalized each letter with script and language, to imply to its recipients that the decree only pertained to the Jews residing in that location. It was thus unlikely that individual communities would comprehend that this was part of an empire-wide genocide, which could lead them to dissent.

To further conceal his plot from the king, and from the Jews – who would rally to defend themselves if given ample advance notice, he sent a supplement to the sealed written edicts, that was to be legally enacted in each province and publicised among all the nations. It stated: “Be militarily prepared for that day – the 13th of Adar. But the scrolls themselves are not to be opened before the 13th of Adar”.
In this way, nobody would know in advance that the Jews were the target.

Finally, only once the high-speed couriers had been dispatched was the law enacted in the Shushan fortress lest the locals discover the plot and lobby the king to block it.
Oblivious to the genocidal nature of the new law, the king sat with Haman to drink wine – which would have otherwise been culturally proscribed, since no one drank wine and sentenced to death on the same day.
And the population of wider Shushan – beyond the fortress – was intrigued by the mysterious new decree.

Despite Haman’s efforts to conceal the Jewish genocide, Mordechai knew everything that had transpired. And Mordechai’s response began with humble repentance to G-d; he tore his clothes and donned sackcloth and ashes. Then he went through the city centre, and screamed loudly and bitterly, to draw attention to the evil decree and publicize its contents to the masses.
Then he went to publicize the decree in the palace, by making a scene as he approached the royal gate. But he did not enter through it, for one may not enter the royal gate wearing sackcloth.

And as Mordechai had intended, the bitter news spread throughout the empire; it reached each province even if not each town and village.
And, in those places in every province that news of the discrepancy between the king’s actual words and the text of Haman’s decree reached, there was great mourning among the Jews, with fasting, weeping, and lamenting; sackcloth and ashes were laid before the masses.
Throughout the empire, the Jews repented and rallied around G-d.

Back at the palace, the chambermaids and valets of Esther came to inform her about Mordechai’s behaviour, and the Queen became very agitated. Immediately, she sent fresh clothes in which to dress Mordechai so that his sackcloth would not be externally visible. Then, he could enter the palace and explain the situation to her. However, he refused the clothing, lest dressing up for the court distract him – albeit momentarily – from his penitence.

Seeing that there was no way to bring Mordechai into the palace, Esther summoned Hatach, the valet that the king had assigned as her personal aide, and the member of the palace staff whom she trusted most.
She instructed him to inquire about Mordechai’s behaviour and message, and to define for her what the problem was, and what its underlying causes were. She hoped to gather enough information to understand the nature of the issue, and how to go about fixing it.
And so Hatach went out to Mordechai, to the city square in front of the royal gate.

Fortunately, Mordechai trusted him and told him directly everything he needed to know; how it all related to his personal encounters with Haman, where he had refused to bow to him. He also told him about the scandalous saga with the silver; how Haman had misled Ahasuerus with his ambiguous smooth talk, and in reality, offered to raise plunder taxation for the royal treasury for the right to “neutralize” the Jews.

And he also handed him the supplementary proclamation to the sealed written edict that had been delivered to Shushan – whose true intent was to annihilate the Jews – to show to Esther and explain the situation to her.
He requested that Hatach instruct Esther to go to the king and beg for his favour, and to plead before him on behalf of her nation.
Armed with this information, Hatach came back to the palace and delivered Mordechai’s message to Esther.

Esther relayed the following reply to Hatach, and instructed him to indirectly forward it to Mordechai. He dared not speak to Mordechai in person for a second time, lest Haman’s men suspect that Mordechai is in cahoots with the queen.

“I do not think it is sensible for me to force entry into the king’s court at this time.
Firstly, all the king’s courtiers and all the civilians in the king’s provinces know that if any man or woman – and that includes me – enters the king’s presence in the inner court without a summons, there is but one directive for him – there are no exceptional extenuating circumstances. He will be put to death! That is, unless the king extends the golden sceptre to him, in which case he may live.
Moreover, I have not been summoned to visit the king for the last thirty days, and it is likely that he will anyway summon me in the near future!
I therefore believe it is far more sensible to wait a while and gain a secure audience. For, if I force entry, even if the king pardons me, I will have spent his favour before I even get to commence pleading the case of the Jews.”
And the middlemen relayed Esther’s words to Mordechai.

But Mordechai was concerned that Esther’s apparently conscientious arguments veiled a degree of complacency, and so he instructed them to reply to Esther as follows: “Do not let yourself fantasize that your life is untouchable because of the king’s love for you; that you will escape the fate of the Jews in the king’s palace.”

“Because if you remain passively silent at this time, I have no doubt that reprieve and salvation will arise for the Jews from someplace else, but if that happens, you and your family heritage will certainly be ‘neutralized’. And, I disagree with your argument that it is more sensible to wait for the king’s summons, because time is of the essence to beat Haman to the king’s ear – who knows, perhaps it is for this very moment that you miraculously entered the monarchy!
Esther, your ability to escape punishment and charm the royal court despite your disrespectful and secretive conduct is clearly providential. It suggests that you have merited ongoing Divine protection because the fate of your people rests with you. Should you fail to represent your people for even one moment, I fear the probable course of nature will come back with vengeance, and you will be harshly punished.”

Esther, upon appreciating that her life was hanging by a thread regardless of her proposed inaction, and emboldened by Mordechai’s faith that even should her petition fail, the Jews will be saved through other means, instructed that the following reply be sent to Mordechai:

“Go, assemble all the Jews present in Shushan, and fast on my behalf. Do not eat or drink for three days, night or day. I and my chambermaids will similarly fast. And then, I shall go to the king against the law, and even if I am to be ‘neutralized’, at least only I shall be ‘neutralized’, whereas the Jews will find other means of salvation!”
And Mordechai passed through the Jewish quarter, and proclaimed the fast in accordance with all of Esther’s instructions to him.

On the third day of her fasting, Esther dressed herself in royalty; she looked the epitome of majesty. She went and stood in the king’s inner courtyard opposite the door to the king’s quarters. This maximized her chances of being spotted by the king and presented with the golden sceptre. How providential that the king was sitting at that very moment on his royal throne in his royal quarters, and that it was positioned precisely opposite the door. Normally, the throne was positioned in the courtyard when on public duty, and in the hidden recesses of his private quarters when enjoying time off-duty.

Now, when the king saw Esther the Queen humbly waiting in the courtyard, even though she was his beloved queen who, in his opinion, was entitled to barge unannounced into his quarters, she found even more favour in his eyes. So, the king extended the golden sceptre to Esther, that providentially he had at hand even though he was off duty. Then Esther approached the king and touched the tip of the sceptre.

Realizing that if Esther had voluntarily risked her life to see him, something serious must be up, the king said to her, “What threat personally concerns you, Queen Esther? Or, what critical request do you have?”
I don’t promise to fulfil your request if it concerns other people, but I am willing to give up half the empire to look after you”.

But Esther simply replied, “If it is convenient for the king, I request that the king and Haman come today to the feast that I have already prepared for him”.
By inviting Haman to their intimate party, she hoped to demonstrate to Ahasuerus that she had nothing personal against Haman. She simply had to spare her own life along with the lives of those dearest to her – her people. She also hoped to catch Haman off-guard without his advisory team to support him, while the king was inebriated and short-tempered.

Intrigued, the king accepted the invitation and commanded, “Tell Haman to hurry and do Esther’s bidding – this is Esther’s royal order and he has no choice but to obey”. And thus the king and Haman arrived at the feast that Esther had prepared.

At the wine feast, the king asked Esther once again, “What is it that you request for yourself? I have already told you that it shall be granted to you! Or, what critical request do you have on behalf of someone else? I hereby add to my original offer – even if it pertains to no more than half the empire, it shall be fulfilled!”
Esther reflected on this carefully, and responded: “I hesitate to advance my petition, because I only wish to share my personal request and my critical request that relates to others…

… if I as a person find favor in the king’s eyes, and if the king assumes it a good idea to grant me this personal request and implement my critical request on behalf of others.
Since I only want what is best for the king, and I do not know how much he cherishes me, and I cannot predict how he will take to my request, I dare not share it.
But I decided to make it known to the king that there is something big on my mind, and “if indeed I as a person find favor in the king’s eyes, and if indeed the king assumes it will be a good idea to grant me this personal request and implement my critical request on behalf of others”3The first part of this verse is read both forwards and backwards, completing the idea that began in the previous verse, while introducing the idea introduced later in this verse., then the king and Haman shall come to another feast that I shall prepare for them, and tomorrow – should the king instruct me to share what is on my mind – I will be obedient and submit to his command.

That day, the power-hungry Haman left the king’s palace happy and lighthearted. He had finally achieved the status that he so coveted – he was on par with the royals!
But as soon as Haman saw Mordechai at the royal gates, who would neither rise nor stir before him, he became filled with inward grievance at Mordechai once more.
Haman thought to himself: “Even if he will not bow before me for religious reasons, how dare he not flinch? Does he not realize that I can have him killed for disobedience? He clearly underestimates me! He thinks that I am a powerless nobody!”
Haman repressed his urge to immediately report Mordechai’s misdemeanours to the king, and instead went home, whereupon he sent for his admirers and Zeresh his wife.

Haman presented the assembled council with his dilemma. He told them about his staggering successes: His great wealth, his many sons, and all that the king had done to promote him and advance him above all the other officials and courtiers.

“Moreover”, said Haman, “Queen Esther did not invite anyone besides the king and myself to the feast that she made. And tomorrow too I am invited by her along with the king.
She has this big request to make of the king, and so she invited me to back her up and influence the king in her favor! Evidently, I am the most influential man in the empire!”

“Yet, all this grandeur is worthless to me each time I see Mordechai the Jew sitting at the royal gate. As much as I would love to punish him, due to my very greatness, it is beneath my dignity to take his disrespectfulness to heart.”

His wife Zeresh and all his admirers expressed the following advice to him, “Let them make use of the stake that is fifty cubits high.”
On this stake, lower-class petty criminals were executed without trial and their corpses publicly displayed, to strike terror into the hearts of the populace.
“Then, early in the morning, when the fresh corpses are displayed to greet people on their way to work, ask the king to hang Mordechai on it – precisely because he is a lower-class petty criminal. By executing him in this manner, you will emphasize that the nature of his crime was of little consequence. Thus, you can exact vengeance from Mordechai while maintaining a guise of indifference.
And then you can accompany the king to the feast happily.”
The proposal seemed good in the eyes of Haman, and he made the stake.

That night, sleep evaded the king. He was intrigued by Esther’s request. “What could she want? She claimed that she had his best interests in mind? Last time she looked out for him, it was to foil the plot of Bigtan and Teresh?!” To attempt to second-guess her, he called for his personal diary, and had the entries read out before him.
How providential that he opted for his personal diary rather than the state chronicles, since those had likely been revised by Haman to give himself the credit at Mordechai’s expense.

And Ahasuerus found something that caught his eye; that it was Mordechai who had informed on Bigtan and Teresh – two of the king’s valets tasked with guarding the threshold to his quarters – who had plotted to attack King Ahasuerus.
The king had totally forgotten about Mordechai’s role, and assumed that his confidantes and especially Haman had been involved in foiling the plot.

And so the king said, “Which lavish reward shall we bestow on Mordechai, and which promotion shall we offer him – on account of this deed? He is already a courtier on Esther’s account, but his loyalty deserves more public attention.” But the king’s young menservants dismissively replied: “Let us offer him nothing at all.”

Just then, the king was informed that there was a visitor in his outer courtyard. The king asked, “Who is in the courtyard?”
How providential and ironic that precisely at that moment Haman came to the king’s outer courtyard to advise the king to hang Mordechai as an inconsequential petty criminal, on the stake that he had prepared for him.

The king’s young menservants answered him, “It is Haman standing in the court.”
“Let him enter,” said the king.

And Haman entered, whereupon the king said to him, “What should be done for a man whom the king desires to lavishly reward?” The king deliberately omitted “and promote”, so that Haman would assume he is the likely lucky recipient, and thus his answer would be neither defensive nor envious.
And, as the king had surmised, Haman said to himself, “Whom could the king desire to honour more than me?”
After pondering over it, Haman replied to the king with fake humility: “The greatest reward is the knowledge that one is a person whom the king wishes to honour.”

That said, in order to publicize the king’s admiration, let the courtiers bring royal dress that the king himself wore, and a horse on which the king himself rode on his coronation day – upon which the royal crown was set on his head.

Then, place the royal dress and the horse in the charge of one of the king’s most noble courtiers. Then, have the courtiers attire the man whom the king desires to lavishly reward, and parade him on the horse through the city square and proclaim before him: “Such is done for the man whom the king desires to lavishly reward!”

The king was deeply concerned by Haman’s megalomaniac fantasy to blur the boundaries between himself and the king; “Haman must be put in his place; it is time to divest some of his powers to trustworthy Mordechai who had proved his fidelity to the king.”
And so the king said to Haman, “Hurry, I order you to personally take the royal dress and the horse exactly as you said, and I insist that you personally perform this entire ceremony – from the dressing through the parading – for Mordechai the Jew who sits at the royal gate. Do not omit a single detail from what you just described to me!”

So Haman took the royal dress and the horse. He personally dressed Mordechai and paraded him through the city square. He personally proclaimed before him: “Such is done for the man whom the king desires to lavishly reward!”

How providential that this episode achieved precisely the opposite of what Haman had in mind. Ultimately, Mordechai returned unharmed to the royal gate, while Haman was sent home, mournfully, hanging his head in shame.

Haman related the unlucky fate that had befallen him to his wife Zeresh and all his admirers. He hoped they would allay his fear that Mordechai had now become invulnerable. He hoped they would agree that this was an insignificant stroke of bad luck. But, to his dismay, his sage counsellors and even his wife Zeresh replied: “If Mordechai, before whom you have fallen by your own initiative and doing, is a scion of the Jews – the people of providence, you’d best leave him alone. You will not overcome him; you will plummet long before he does.”

How providential that while they were still speaking with him, the king’s valets arrived and overheard Haman’s ongoing megalomaniac ambitions that included deposing Mordechai. They harried Haman, for they had orders to quickly bring him to the banquet that Esther had prepared.

Esther’s strategy had been right on the mark. The king, following his sleepless night of intrigue, decided to trust Esther. He would order her to share her request, and he was certain that he could grant it. And so, on the back of an eventful 24-hours for both the king and Haman, they arrived at the feast that Esther had made.

As she had hoped, the king again said to Esther, at the wine feast on this second day: “What is your personal request – o Esther the queen whom I love dearly and whose concerns I obviously wish to address – and it shall be granted to you, and what is your critical request on behalf of others – that shall be fulfilled even if it pertains to up to half the empire!

And now Esther the queen responded and said, “If I find favor in your eyes – o King whom I esteem and for whom I only request the best – and if it seems good in the king’s eyes: Let my very life be granted to me for my personal request, and the very lives of my people for my critical other-focused request.

For none less than I, as well as my people, have been sold to a treacherous tyrant, to be annihilated, murdered, and “neutralized”. My majesty, you were misled: The tyrant wants blood, not just religious-cultural reformation. And the supposedly insignificant people in his crosshairs are none other than the virtuous Jews. Moreover, I fear that this heinous genocide is all my fault; that the tyrant’s entire scheme is just a pretext to depose me. Had we just been sold to become slaves and maids I would have remained silent, so as not to trouble the king. But, as we have been sold for annihilation, it is this tyrant who is not worth the trouble he causes the king, rather than the people about whom he slanderously claimed, ‘it is not worth the king’s while to let them be’.”

Upon hearing this, King Ahasuerus turned to his aides, and upon their shocked silence, turned to Esther the queen, “Who is the person with such a despicable scheme? And what is the underlying motivation, that the person convinced themselves of the feasibility of such unfathomable action?”

Whereupon Esther said, “Indeed, ‘a tyrannical and hateful man’ perfectly describes this evil Haman. He is a person with despicable character – he is a dishonest, cruel and narcissistic megalomaniac, who develops profound and deep-seated hatred towards anyone who crosses his path.”
Haman was panic stricken as he was faced by both the king and the queen. He had been exposed, and whatever he could muster in his defense would only make matters worse. To justify his hatred of the Jews would further provoke the queen, and to double down on his plot would confirm that he had lied to the king!

The king, overwhelmed by his internal aggrievment that he had been tricked by his closest advisor and was now stuck in a bureaucratic nightmare with the life of his queen on the line, arose from the wine feast and headed for the palace garden. Haman remained to plead for his life from Esther the queen, because he saw that, from the king’s perspective, his nasty fate was sealed.

When the king returned from the palace garden to the chamber in which the wine feast was held, to his horror he found that Haman had collapsed on the couch on which Esther was reclined. Presuming that Esther had correctly surmised that Haman wished to depose her, he interpreted Haman’s behaviour as a last-ditch attempt to murder her. And so the king furiously declared, “He even attempts to overthrow the queen in my very presence in the palace!”
As soon as these words left the king’s mouth, they covered Haman’s face in accordance with Persian tradition that when the king is angry with you, make sure not to be seen.

And then Charvona, one of the king’s valets, who had been sent to escort Haman to the feast and had thus overheard Haman’s plot to assassinate Mordechai, spoke up and said: “There is further incriminating evidence from the stake that Haman has made for Mordechai who spoke-up for the king’s benefit when Bigtan and Teresh plotted to assassinate him. Surely Haman’s animosity towards Mordechai confirms that he was party to this plot? Moreover, even though the king has now publicly paraded Mordechai and instructed his promotion, it is still standing in Haman’s home, and he still intends to use it. He does not care that it would publicly humiliate the king if Mordechai was hanged as a petty criminal!”
The king had heard enough and ordered: “Hang him on it instead!”
And so they hanged Haman on the tree that he had prepared for Mordechai, and the inner aggrievement of the king was calmed.

Within the space of one day, all of Haman’s power and prestige was handed over to his primary adversary:
That very day King Ahasuerus gave the estate of Haman, the arch persecutor of the Jews, to Queen Esther. Had the king executed him for treason against the king, his property would have belonged to the king. This gesture communicated that Haman was primarily executed for treason against the queen, fuelled by his Jew hatred. And Mordechai was promoted such that he could present himself to the king whenever he pleased, for, in addition to his virtues, Esther had revealed how he was related to her.
The king removed his signet ring that he had reclaimed from Haman, and gave it to Mordechai. Esther put Mordechai in charge of Haman’s estate.

Despite the king’s magnanimous gestures to protect Esther, he had not indicated any willingness to spare the Jews from their fate. Esther appreciated that Ahasuerus was faced with an acute bureaucratic dilemma – Persian etiquette prohibited backtracking on an established law. And while the dictatorial Ahasuerus had no regard for the legal tradition, he certainly did not want to come across as unethical or uncouth.
Worried that he was avoiding her request, Esther continued her plea. She reasoned with the king to influence him intellectually, and she fell at his feet and wept to influence him emotionally.
She beseeched him to avert the evil decree of Haman the Agagite and the scheme that he intended for the Jews.
She argued that standard etiquette did not apply. Firstly, the edict was issued by Haman and not the king – who had been utterly misled; this could hardly be called backtracking. Secondly, since the scrolls were presently unopened, recalling them would not constitute backtracking on established legislation.
The king extended the golden sceptre to Esther to communicate his willingness to listen further, and so Esther arose and stood before the king.

And this is what she said:
“If:
a) My petition is emotionally attractive –
a. its content appeals to the king;
b. I, the petitioner, appeal to the king;
b) My plan is strategically sound –
a. It seems ethically correct to the king. By dissociating himself with such an evil plot while working within the confines of existing etiquette, news of the king’s ethicality would spread across the empire;
b. I am sufficiently valuable in his eyes to ensure that I, the queen, do not become a depressed or insane woman –
Then:
Let an edict be written that all the scrolls containing the scheme of Haman son of Hammedata the Agagite be returned, those in which he wrote to “neutralize” the Jews throughout all the king’s provinces.”

“And the Jews’ safety cannot be secured by appending a second sealed scroll to be opened on the 13th of Adar that will qualify the intention of the first scroll, for how can I cope with beholding the evil that will likely befall my people in the interim now that news of the first scroll’s contents has leaked and the Jews are already perceived as dead-men walking, and how can I cope with beholding the possible demolition of my entire heritage!? How can I be confident that the masses will appreciate legal subtlety, and correctly reinterpret the first scroll in light of the second?

The king rejected Esther’s first plan but was willing to pursue her second plan. He believed it would be both ethically viable and sufficiently effective.
This is what King Ahasuerus replied to Esther the queen and Mordechai the Jew: Look, I have already handed Haman’s estate to Esther and hanged him on the stake for his attempt to harm the Jews. Does this not broadcast that Haman abused my trust and acted against my Jewish queen? Haven’t my actions already undermined the credibility of the first scroll? Won’t the masses now read the scrolls very carefully to ensure that their behaviour towards the Jews is lawful?

I suggest that you write a second scroll to clarify and reinterpret the wording of the first edict, in such a manner that you deem favourable to the Jews.
Perhaps transform the Jews from the object to the subject by adding clarification as follows:
To destroy, massacre, and neutralize
–TO BE IMPLEMENTED BY –
all the Jews,
–TO BE IMPLEMENTED ON THEIR ENEMY –
from the young to the old, children and women.
Write this clarification in the name of the king and sign it with the royal signet. Because, in my opinion, even in circumstances such as these, an edict that has been previously written in the king’s name and signed with the king’s signet may not be recalled.

Some time thereafter, in the third month of the Jewish calendar, that is on the twenty-third day of Sivan, the king’s scribes were summoned. Mordechai and Esther decided to wait until the couriers had returned from delivering the first scrolls so that they could use the same couriers to deliver the second scrolls. This would increase the credibility of the second scrolls and prove that they were not forged.
The scrolls were written as per Mordechai’s instructions and addressed to the Jews, the king’s satraps and governors, and the officials of every one of the 127 nations from India to North-West Africa. They wrote to every province in its own script and to every people in their own language. They also addressed the Jews in their own script and their own language.
The second scrolls were more widely disseminated than the first scrolls issued by Haman. This time, there were additional scrolls uniquely addressed to the Jews, and scrolls sent to local officials across the entire breadth of the empire. Conversely, Haman had sufficed with sending scrolls to the main regional authorities in the more far-flung reaches of the empire. The addition of new addressees who had not received the first scroll would further establish the second scroll’s primacy over the first.

Mordechai wrote the new edicts in the name of King Ahasuerus and sealed them with the king’s signet. He dispatched them as scrolls with high-speed couriers riding on horseback with the select steeds of the royal stables.

And this is what they proclaimed: “That the king had granted permission to the Jews in each and every city to congregate and rise-up to fight for their lives. They may destroy, massacre, and “neutralize” any armies of all peoples and provinces that persecute them, along with their women and children.
And, they may plunder their possessions –

But only on that single day, on the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, that is, the month of Adar.
Whereas Haman’s edict implied that there was no deadline for the plunder – to encourage people to murder as many Jews as possible on the 13th and plunder afterwards – Mordechai’s edict expressly limited the plunder to the 13th as well. The reason for this was that Mordechai thought it distasteful for the Jews to plunder. By limiting the right to plunder to the day when the Jews would be otherwise occupied with killing their enemies, he effectively ensured that they wouldn’t act on this right.
Moreover, Mordechai emphasized in each scroll that this edict was disseminated and applied in all the provinces of King Ahasuerus. Hopefully, this would counter Haman’s attempt to conceal the widespread genocidal nature of the edict in the first scroll.
In summation, this is what the second scroll looked like, with Mordechai’s qualifications capitalized and italicized:
–TO : ALL THE KING’S SATRAPS AND GOVERNORS, AND THE OFFICIALS OF EVERY ONE OF THE 127 NATIONS FROM INDIA TO NORTH-WEST AFRICA –
You are hereby instructed:
To destroy, massacre, and neutralize
–TO BE IMPLEMENTED BY –
all the Jews,
–TO BE IMPLEMENTED ON THEIR ENEMY –
from the young to the old, children and women.
–AND TO PLUNDER THEIR POSSESSIONS –
on a single day, on the thirteenth day of the twelfth month – that is, the month of Adar.

He also sent a supplement to the sealed written edicts, that was to be legally enacted in each province and publicised among all the nations. It stated: The Jews shall be militarily prepared for that day – the 13th of Adar – to exact revenge from their enemies. But, once again, the scrolls themselves were not to be opened before the 13th of Adar.

The couriers, riding the select steeds of the royal stables, departed in a state of confusion and frenzy at the king’s command; and only once they had left, the law was enacted in the capital Shushan. Like Haman before him, Mordechai wanted to ensure that the edicts were dispatched before local lobbyists could become aware of their contents and petition the king to block them.

Only once he secured his people’s future did Mordechai go public with his newfound status. Mordechai then went out from the king’s presence in royal robes of indigo-blue and white cotton, with a large crown of gold and a mantle of fine linen and purple. And the entire wider city of Shushan – Jewish and non-Jewish inhabitants alike – rang with joyous cries and was delighted that megalomanic Haman had been replaced by pious Mordechai.
As for the Jews, they enjoyed light and happiness; they rejoiced and were honoured.

And in every province and in every city – since Mordechai’s scrolls were dispatched to each and every city, to ensure a wider coverage than those of Haman – wherever the king’s command and edict arrived, there was happiness and rejoicing among the Jews, and celebratory feasts and religious holidays were declared. Many of the other peoples of those lands wished they were Jews, for the fear of the Jews fell upon them.
Thus, the plan of Ahasuerus succeeded in quelling any interim uprisings against the Jews; Esther’s concerns that the Jews would be subject to abuses even before the 13th of Adar were allayed.

On the thirteenth day of the twelfth month—that is, the month of Adar, the scrolls were opened. The king’s edicts inscribed in them reached the masses and it was time to act upon them.
How providential that on the very day that the enemies of the Jews had hoped to overcome them, the opposite happened; the Jews were the ones who overcame their enemies.
One of the hallmarks of providence is when a scheme turns on its head; when, not only does it fail to accomplish its aims, but it actually accomplishes the very opposite of its aims. First Haman, and now all the Jew haters met their ends in this very providential fashion.

Providentially, the legal mess caused by the two scrolls paralyzed the enemies of the Jews into inaction, and they encountered no organized resistance.
The Jews who were clearly entitled by the second scroll to hunt down their persecutors congregated in their cities, throughout the provinces of King Ahasuerus, to attack those who sought to harm them.
Conversely, the Jew-haters were confused by the mixed messages: Was the second scroll an addition to the first, or a reinterpretation of the first? Were both the Jew-haters and the Jews permitted to attack one another, or were the Jews alone permitted to attack? Thus, no layman resisted them, for their awe had befallen all the peoples, leading them to err on the side of caution.

Moreover, in all the fortified cities and centres of local government, the officials of the provinces, the satraps, the governors, and members of the king’s civil service, promoted the Jews and their cause. This was not because they particularly loved the Jews, but because fear of Mordechai befell them.
Despite their doubts as to the legality of the second scroll which for all intents and purposes revoked an earlier law, Mordechai’s intentions were clear and nobody dared to mess with him.

For over the course of the year, Mordechai had become an impressive presence in running the king’s palace, and word of his political acumen spread throughout the provinces. Moreover, Mordechai’s personal status spread continually abroad, upon successfully devising and directing military campaigns.

And so, on the 13th, encountering no military resistance, the Jews subjected their openly declared enemies who had a persecutory track-record to the sword, death and “neutralization”, and behaved towards their covert haters as they pleased.
While the edict only sanctioned killing those who had actively persecuted the Jews, the political climate enabled the harassment and subjugation of all Jew-haters.
In Shushan, the capital city, the Jews killed five hundred men –
Along with: Parshandata, Dalfon, Aspata,
Porata, Adalia, Aridata,
Parmashta, Arisai, Aridai, and Vaizata –

the ten sons of Haman son of Hammedata, arch persecutor of the Jews. And in accordance with Mordechai’s implied wishes, they did not lay their hands on the spoils. They acted purely out of self-defence, without lust and greed.
On that day, the vast number of the openly persecutory Jew-haters who had been slain was brought to the king’s attention.

The king, shocked at their vast numbers, said to Esther the queen: “If in Shushan the capital – under my very nose – the Jews executed and neutralized five hundred actively persecutory Jew-hating men besides the sons of Haman, how did they fare in my other royal provinces where they likely faced much stiffer resistance? Your position is still vulnerable; Do you have any further personal requests – they shall be granted to you! Do you have any further critical requests on behalf of others – they shall be implemented!

Esther wisely requested: “If it seems good to the king, let the Jews in wider Shushan – outside the fortress city – be permitted to act tomorrow as they did today; and let Haman’s ten executed sons be impaled on the stake for all to see.
By indicating that your protection of the Jews extends beyond the one-off edict of the 13th of Adar, and by hanging arch Jew-haters such as Haman’s sons on the royal stakes, news of the king’s ongoing support for the Jewish cause will be spread far and wide, and suppress the malice in the hearts of the remaining Jew-haters.”
The king agreed with Esther’s strategy and ordered its implementation, and the edict was asserted in Shushan. And so, Haman’s ten sons were hanged.
And then the Jews in Shushan gathered again on the 14th day of Adar and killed a further three hundred men in Shushan. Once again, they did not lay their hands on the spoils.

Indeed, Ahasuerus’ concerns for the fate of the rest of the Jews throughout the king’s provinces – especially those living outside fortified cities who did not enjoy the protection of the local government and royal garrison stationed there – were not ill-founded. They gathered and fought for their lives against organized militias of Jew-haters until eventually they were relieved of their overt enemies. In the course of fighting, they overstepped the boundaries of the law and killed a further seventy-five thousand of their covert haters – those presumed to possess Amalekite roots. But despite taking this legal liberty, they did not lay hands on the spoils.

The fierce combat, the Jews’ triumph and the Amalek assassinations, all took place on the 13th day of the month of Adar. Then they rested on the 14th of the month, declaring it a day of feasting and celebration.
Conversely, the Jews in Shushan gathered on both the 13th and 14th of the month, and so they only rested on the 15th, declaring it a day of feasting and celebration.

Given the above fortunate military victory, the diaspora Jews who lived in the unwalled towns experienced the 13th of Adar as a day of salvation – the day on which they were spared from death at the hands of Jew-hating militias. Hence, they began to annually observe the 14th day of the month of Adar as a day of celebration and feasting and a religious holiday, on which they send gifts to one another.
Meanwhile, the Jews in the fortified cities were unaware how precarious their situation had been even after the sending of the second scrolls. They did not realize that if not for the fear of Mordechai, a much more deadly interpretation of the scrolls may have been adopted. Thus, from their perspective, nothing particularly noteworthy transpired on the 13th of Adar – the true salvation from their perspective occurred earlier, as soon as Mordechai replaced Haman and sent the second scrolls.

Because they failed to appreciate the full picture, Mordechai recorded these events and dispatched them as scrolls to all the Jews throughout the provinces of King Ahasuerus, both near and far. It was important to him that all the Jews fully appreciate the true extent of their salvation on the 13th of Adar.
And he instructed them to adopt the existing practice of the village Jews and observe the 14th and 15th days of Adar each and every year.

On the corresponding days on which they had enjoyed relief from their overt enemies – that is, on the 14th or 15th – during the month that had been transformed for them from one to be associated with grief to one associated with happiness, and from one to be associated with mourning to one associated with religious festivities. He instructed them to express this happiness by instituting these dates as days for feasting, celebration and sending gifts to one another, and to express the religious undertones of this festival by donating charitable presents to the poor.
Mordechai taught them that it is against Jewish law to add religious festivals with classical festival flavour to those explicitly mentioned in the Torah. Therefore, they must adopt this new avenue for expressing the religious character of the day.

And all the Jews accepted upon themselves to abide by what they had already begun to do in the diaspora beyond the fortified cities and to conduct themselves in accordance with the Torah-legal guidance in the writings of Mordechai to them.

Because Mordechai’s scrolls made unequivocally clear how Haman son of Hammedata the Agagite, was in fact the arch persecutor of all the Jews, and how while he had initially plotted to “neutralize” the religion and culture of the Jews alone, he upon casting the pur – that is, the lot – became increasingly superstitious and determined to crush and exterminate them.

And how even when Esther came before the king to beseech him to recall Haman’s decree, he refused to do so and instead commanded: “The evil plot must be turned on its head without invalidating the first scroll, and that is why they hanged him and his sons on the stake.
How scare tactics were necessary precisely because the first scroll had ongoing legal; how the Jew-haters largely ignoring the first edict was very fortunate.

For this reason – namely, the utter reversal of the fortunes of Haman and the Jews – they called these days “Purim” – lots.
And because of all the contents of this letter that clarified the providence behind the events they had seen, and the fate that actually befell them –

They formalized and accepted upon themselves and their descendants, and upon all who join them stipulating that it be an irrevocable religious commitment, to observe these two days, each year, at the proper time – the 14th for unfortified settlements and the 15th for fortified settlements – centred around their writings that shall be publicly read on these days.

And indeed these days are recalled through reading this scroll and observed through celebration, feasts and gifts, in every generation, in every family, in every diaspora province, and in every fortified city. And due to the stipulation of irrevocability, these days of Purim shall never be removed from the Jews’ calendar, and their memory shall never die out among their descendants.
POSTSCRIPT:

But it was not plain sailing – there was one further hurdle to overcome. Religious-legal controversy broke out whether this scroll was worthy of canonization, and whether it was acceptable to tamper with the Sinaitic Torah by formally establishing a new religious holiday.
Mordechai and Esther so firmly believed in the value of the scroll and the feasibility of the new holiday, that Queen Esther daughter of Avichayil and Mordechai the Jew used their combined royal and religious authorities and wrote an affidavit confirming the validity of the complete Purim document in its second edition – that added this postscript alluding to the controversy and Mordechai and Esther’s emphatic response.

And Mordechai dispatched the second edition of the scrolls to all the Jews in the hundred and twenty-seven provinces of Ahasuerus’s empire, emphasizing that they are words that are both diplomatic and true. They apologized for exercising secular political power, emphasizing that they were compelled to do so to uphold the religious truth and preserve Jewish unity.

And they explained the crux of their argument: That these days of Purim shall be formally observed at their proper times by man-made commitment, just as Mordechai the Jew and Esther the queen had committed themselves, and just as Jews have committed themselves and their descendants to formally observing the fast days with their lamentations. Their thesis was convincing: It is permissible to add religious holidays and fast-days to the Jewish calendar if they are clearly stipulated as man-made bottom-up customs, and not top-down Divinely-communicated laws.
And Esther’s thesis was successful; it validated these matters concerning the Purim festival, and had the story included in the written canon.
Assisted by Mordechai’s wise counsel, King Ahasuerus’ influence spread far and wide; he imposed tribute on many regions of the mainland as well as the isles of the seas.

And, if you are looking for a full account of his might and power, as inspired by Mordechai, and the resultant greatness bestowed upon Mordechai by the king, surely you will find that they are recorded in the Annals of the kings of Media and Persia.

For Mordechai the Jew remained second in command to King Ahasuerus, enjoying a long tenure. He successfully governed all the empire’s provinces and nations, and of course, the Jews. Although he was faithful to the king’s interests, he was highly regarded by most of his kin, because it was widely recognized that he sought the good of his people and spoke of peace for all its generations.
